# Episode 1: Kicking the Tires on "AI-Native"
## "Why AI Diligence Now, and How to Test an AI Claim"

**Duration:** ~49 minutes
**Hosts:** Nadia & Owen
**Podcast:** The AI Diligence Room

---

### Cold open

[INTRO MUSIC]

**NADIA:** A management presentation. Slide fourteen. A big, confident headline: "Our AI platform automates eighty percent of the work." A chart going up and to the right. A logo wall of happy customers.

**OWEN:** And the question every deal team should ask at that moment is very simple. Eighty percent of what work, measured how, by whom, and since when?

**NADIA:** Welcome to The AI Diligence Room, the show about buying companies in a world where every seller has an AI story. I'm Nadia.

**OWEN:** And I'm Owen. Over four long episodes, we're going to work through AI diligence the way a deal team actually does it. Today, why AI diligence matters now, and how to test an AI claim. Next time, the data, the models and the technology stack underneath the claim. In episode three, the other side of the coin: whether AI threatens the target's business. And in episode four, how all of those findings turn into price, contract terms and a plan for the first hundred days.

**NADIA:** Our usual note on sources. Everything we cite is public: regulatory actions, court filings, published research and press coverage. When we describe a company that's been charged or sued, we'll be careful to say what's alleged versus what's been proven. And when we use an example target to walk through a process, it's made up.

**OWEN:** And this isn't legal or investment advice. It's a practitioner's map. Your counsel, your accountants and your own judgment do the rest.

---

### Why AI diligence, why now

**NADIA:** Let's start with the obvious question. Diligence has always covered technology. Why does AI need its own treatment?

**OWEN:** Three reasons. The first is that AI changed the value of a lot of businesses very quickly, in both directions. Bain's midyear private equity report this year described what it called a triple shock, and the first part of that was an AI-driven selloff in software valuations. Public markets started pricing in the possibility that AI agents would eat into seat-based software, information services and outsourced services. When the market moves that fast, the deal team has to have a view on where a target sits.

**NADIA:** So AI can be a threat to the asset.

**OWEN:** A threat to some assets and a tailwind to others. That's the second half of the first reason. A company that uses AI well can expand margins, grow faster with less hiring, and widen its lead on competitors. So the same technology can make one target worth more and another worth less, and the deal team needs to tell them apart.

**NADIA:** Second reason.

**OWEN:** Claims. Every seller now has an AI story, because sellers know buyers will pay for one. Some of those stories are excellent and well-evidenced. Some are a thin layer of AI on a conventional business. And a few, as we'll see, have turned out to be false in ways that regulators and prosecutors have acted on. The buyer's job is to tell which is which before signing, not after.

**NADIA:** And the third.

**OWEN:** New risks that don't fit neatly into the old diligence workstreams. Data rights, model licenses, dependence on a handful of AI providers, regulatory exposure under new AI laws, security risks specific to AI systems, and insurance. Representations and warranties insurers are starting to exclude AI-specific risks, according to Foley. If the diligence doesn't cover those risks well, the buyer may find they're neither insured nor protected in the contract.

**NADIA:** So three questions for every target.

**OWEN:** Three questions. Is AI a threat to this business? Is the target's AI story true and durable? And what new risks come with the AI the target uses? We'd add a fourth, which is the opportunity: how much value could we create with AI after we own it? That one feeds the value creation plan and, often, the price we're willing to pay.

---

### The four questions in practice

**NADIA:** Let's turn that into a framework a deal team can use. Walk me through each question.

**OWEN:** I call them threat, claim, risk and upside. Threat asks: if AI keeps improving at the current pace for the next five years, does this business's revenue get stronger or weaker? Who are its customers, what do they pay for, and could an AI system, or a competitor using one, do that more cheaply?

**NADIA:** That's a strategic question more than a technical one.

**OWEN:** Mostly strategic, which is why it belongs with the commercial diligence team, not only the technology advisors. We'll spend all of episode three on it. Claim asks: what does the target say about its AI, and is it true? That's partly technical, partly commercial and partly financial. Risk asks: what could go wrong with the target's AI that would cost us money, in legal exposure, regulatory fines, security incidents or reputation? And upside asks: what would we do with AI after closing, and how confident are we in the value?

**NADIA:** Does every deal need all four in depth?

**OWEN:** No. The depth should match the deal. For a software company whose valuation depends on its AI product, you go very deep on claim and risk, and threat is existential. For a regional HVAC business, the claim is probably small, the threat is low, the risk is mostly about the vendors they use, and the upside is the big question. That's the Real Economy show's territory, which some of you will have heard.

**NADIA:** So step one is scoping.

**OWEN:** Step one is a quick triage, ideally before the first management meeting. Read the teaser and the information memorandum, count how many times AI is mentioned, see where in the value story it sits, and decide which of the four questions matters most. If the seller's projections assume an AI product launch drives a third of growth, the claim question is central. If the target is a call center outsourcer, the threat question is.

---

### What AI-washing looks like

**NADIA:** Let's talk about the claim question, because it's where the headlines are. What's AI-washing?

**OWEN:** AI-washing is overstating what AI does in a business, or claiming AI where there isn't much. It's named after greenwashing, and it ranges from harmless marketing exaggeration to outright fraud.

**NADIA:** And regulators have acted on it.

**OWEN:** They have, several times now, which is useful for diligence because it shows the patterns. In March 2024, the Securities and Exchange Commission settled charges against two investment advisers, Delphia and Global Predictions, for making false and misleading statements about their use of AI. The penalties were modest, a few hundred thousand dollars in total, but the SEC chair at the time made a point of the message: if you claim to use AI, it had better be true.

**NADIA:** That was investment advisers. What about operating companies?

**OWEN:** In January 2025, the SEC settled charges against Presto Automation, a company that sold AI voice ordering systems to restaurant drive-thrus. The SEC said Presto had made misleading statements about its technology, including about how much human intervention was needed. According to the SEC, the large majority of drive-thru orders taken by its system required human intervention by staff working off site, and the company hadn't disclosed that clearly. The company settled without admitting or denying the findings.

**NADIA:** That's a very specific pattern. The AI is real, but there are humans behind it.

**OWEN:** The human-in-the-loop that isn't disclosed. It's one of the most common patterns, and it's not always fraud. Many AI products legitimately use people to check or correct the AI's work. The problem is when the company tells investors or customers that the system is fully automated, and the economics depend on that being true. Because if humans are doing a big share of the work, the gross margin and the scalability are very different from what the pitch implies.

**NADIA:** And there have been criminal cases.

**OWEN:** A few. In 2024, federal prosecutors charged the founder of Joonko, a recruiting startup, with defrauding investors, alleging she'd made false claims about customers and revenue in a company that marketed itself on AI. And in April 2025, prosecutors charged Albert Saniger, the founder of a shopping app called Nate, alleging that he told investors the app used AI to complete online purchases automatically, when in fact, according to the charges, the purchases were largely completed by human workers in a call center. Those are allegations, and the cases go through the courts. But they show what prosecutors look for.

**NADIA:** And the consumer side?

**OWEN:** The Federal Trade Commission ran what it called Operation AI Comply in September 2024, bringing actions against several companies for deceptive AI claims to consumers, including a company that marketed itself as a robot lawyer. The FTC has said repeatedly that there's no AI exemption from the laws against deceptive claims.

**NADIA:** And the collapses?

**OWEN:** The one that got the most attention in 2025 was Builder.ai, a software development company that had raised large amounts from well-known investors on an AI story. It went into insolvency in May 2025, amid reports that its revenue had been significantly overstated. The full story is still being worked out, but for diligence teams, it's a reminder that an AI narrative can distract from basic questions, like whether the revenue is real.

---

### The pattern behind the cases

**NADIA:** So what's the common thread in those cases?

**OWEN:** Four patterns. First, undisclosed humans: the system is described as automated, but people do much of the work. Second, inflated capability: the product works in a demo or for a narrow set of cases, and is described as working broadly. Third, borrowed capability: the company describes a general-purpose model from a big AI provider as its own proprietary technology. And fourth, the oldest one, which is that the AI story is a distraction from the fundamentals, like revenue recognition, customer concentration or cash burn.

**NADIA:** Let's take borrowed capability. That's not fraud, is it?

**OWEN:** Not usually. Building on a foundation model from a major provider is a perfectly sensible strategy. Most good AI products do it. The question for the buyer is where the defensible value is. If the product is a thin layer on someone else's model, sometimes called a wrapper, then two things are at risk. The model provider could add the same feature to its own product, and competitors can build the same thing quickly. What you want to find is the value that doesn't come from the model: proprietary data, deep workflow integration, distribution, customer relationships, regulatory approvals, or a lot of hard-won domain knowledge built into the product.

**NADIA:** And how do you tell?

**OWEN:** Ask the team a simple question: if we swapped the underlying model for a competitor's tomorrow, what would change for the customer? If the answer is "nothing much," the model isn't the moat, which is fine, as long as something else is. If the answer is "everything," then the business depends heavily on one supplier, which is a different risk we'll cover next episode.

**NADIA:** What about inflated capability?

**OWEN:** That's where testing comes in. A demo is a performance. What you want is evidence on real data, at real volumes, with real error rates. We'll talk about how to get that in a minute.

---

### The claim test

**NADIA:** Let's make this practical. Our made-up target is a company called Ledgerline. It sells accounts payable software to mid-sized companies, and its pitch says its AI reads and codes invoices automatically, with "ninety five percent straight-through processing." What does the diligence team do?

**OWEN:** Start by decomposing the claim. "Ninety five percent straight-through processing" sounds like one number, but it's really several. Ninety five percent of what: invoices, invoice lines, or dollar value? For which customers: all of them, or the ones with the cleanest data? Over what time period? And what counts as straight through: no human touch at all, or no human touch by the customer, while the company's own staff check things in the background?

**NADIA:** That last one is the Presto question.

**OWEN:** Exactly. So the second step is to ask for the underlying data. Not a slide, but the operational metrics from the production system. For a product like Ledgerline's, every invoice has a processing history: when it arrived, what the AI extracted, whether anyone edited it, who that person was, and how long it took. That data exists, because the company needs it to run the product. Ask for it, by customer, by month, for the last two years.

**NADIA:** And if they won't share it?

**OWEN:** Then that's a finding. Sometimes there are legitimate confidentiality concerns, and you can address those with a clean room or by having an independent advisor run the analysis. But if a company that claims ninety five percent automation can't produce the data that would prove it, you should weight the claim accordingly.

**NADIA:** And when you get the data?

**OWEN:** Look at the distribution, not the average. Is the ninety five percent driven by a few big customers with very standard invoices, while smaller customers are at sixty percent? Is it rising over time, flat, or falling? What happens to new customers in their first three months? That tells you about onboarding costs. And look at the staff side: how many people at Ledgerline touch invoices, and how has that number changed as volume grew? If volume tripled and the operations team tripled too, the automation isn't scaling the way the story implies.

**NADIA:** What about the accuracy of the work the AI does?

**OWEN:** That's the third step. Straight through isn't useful if it's wrong. Ask how the company measures accuracy, how often customers correct coded invoices after the fact, and what the error rate is on the things that matter, like amounts, vendor matching and duplicate payments. Ideally, take a random sample of invoices processed automatically and have someone independent check them.

**NADIA:** That sounds like a lot of work.

**OWEN:** It's a few days of focused work for a technical advisor with access to the data, and it can change the valuation. If the real automation rate is seventy percent, not ninety five, the gross margin assumptions in the model are wrong, and so is the cost to scale.

---

### Testing the product yourself

**NADIA:** You said a demo is a performance. Should the deal team test the product directly?

**OWEN:** Where it's feasible, yes. A hands-on test is one of the most informative things you can do, and it's usually cheaper than people think. For Ledgerline, that might mean taking a few hundred real invoices from one of the fund's own portfolio companies, with permission, and running them through the product in a sandbox, then checking the results.

**NADIA:** And for products where that's harder?

**OWEN:** Then you test what you can. For a customer service AI, you can call it or chat with it and try the hard cases. For an AI feature in a vertical software product, you can sit with a customer's team while they use it, ideally a customer that the company didn't hand-pick. For a model the company built itself, you can ask for its evaluation results and the test sets behind them, and have an expert review whether the tests were sensible.

**NADIA:** What makes an evaluation sensible?

**OWEN:** A few things. The test data should be separate from the data the model was trained on, otherwise the model has seen the answers. The test cases should reflect real usage, including the hard and unusual cases, not just the easy ones. The measure should match what the customer cares about. And the results should be tracked over time, so you can see whether changes to the model or the underlying provider made things better or worse.

**NADIA:** And if the company doesn't have evaluations?

**OWEN:** That's a finding too, and a fairly common one in younger companies. It doesn't mean the product is bad. It means the company doesn't know, in a systematic way, whether it's good, and it can't tell when it gets worse. For an AI product company, that's a real gap, because the underlying models change, and without evaluations you're flying blind through each change.

---

### Customer calls

**NADIA:** What about customer references? The seller always gives you a list.

**OWEN:** The seller's list is useful but biased, obviously. I'd always do some calls with customers the seller didn't choose, which you can find through the customer list in the data room, through expert networks, or through your own portfolio companies. And the questions are different when AI is part of the story.

**NADIA:** What do you ask?

**OWEN:** Start with what they actually use. Many customers buy a product with AI features and don't use them, or use only a small part. Ask which AI features they use, how often, and for what. Then ask what changed: did they reduce headcount, handle more volume, get faster, or improve quality? Can they put a number on it? Then ask what goes wrong: how often they correct the AI, what kind of errors they see, and whether they trust it for important work.

**NADIA:** And the renewal question.

**OWEN:** The most important one. Would they renew at a higher price because of the AI? Are they considering alternatives, including building something themselves with a general-purpose AI tool, or using AI features from a bigger vendor they already have? That last one is a growing theme. A customer who says "we're waiting to see what our ERP vendor ships next year" is telling you about the threat.

**NADIA:** And pricing?

**OWEN:** Ask how they'd feel about the vendor changing to usage-based or outcome-based pricing. Many software companies are moving that way because of AI, and customers' reactions vary a lot. Some welcome paying for results. Others hate unpredictable bills. That tells you how much pricing power the company really has.

---

### Management interviews

**NADIA:** And management? What do you ask the leadership team?

**OWEN:** I like to separate the conversations. The CEO tells you the vision. The CTO or head of AI tells you how it works. The CFO tells you how it shows up in the numbers. And the head of customer success or operations tells you what actually happens with customers. If those four stories don't line up, you've learned something.

**NADIA:** Give me some questions for each.

**OWEN:** For the CEO: what share of the company's value do you think comes from AI today, and in three years? What would you do if the largest AI providers launched a competing feature? For the CTO: walk me through the architecture of the AI features. Which models do you use, from whom, and why? How do you evaluate quality? What happened the last time a model provider changed or retired a model you depended on?

**NADIA:** For the CFO.

**OWEN:** What does AI cost you, per customer and per transaction, and how is that trending? Where does it sit in the income statement, cost of revenue or research and development? How much of your revenue comes from AI features or AI-priced products, and how do you define that? And how many people, in operations or support, are involved in delivering AI features to customers?

**NADIA:** And the head of customer success?

**OWEN:** What do customers complain about with the AI? What's the most common reason a customer churns? How much time does onboarding take for the AI features, and who does it? Which customers use the AI the most, and what do they have in common?

**NADIA:** What's a red flag in those interviews?

**OWEN:** A CTO who can't explain clearly how the AI works or how they measure it. A CFO who can't tell you what AI costs. Very different numbers from different people. And defensiveness about access to data. A good team with a real AI product is usually proud to show you the details.

---

### The financial footprint of AI

**NADIA:** Let's go deeper on the CFO's side. How does AI show up in a target's financials?

**OWEN:** In several places, and some of them are easy to miss. The most direct is the cost of running the AI, often called inference cost, which is the bill from the model provider or the cloud provider for each request. For an AI product, that's part of the cost of delivering the service, so it hits gross margin.

**NADIA:** And AI products often have lower gross margins than traditional software.

**OWEN:** Often, yes. Traditional software can have very high gross margins, because serving one more customer costs almost nothing. AI products have a real cost per use, plus sometimes human review costs. Many AI-heavy companies report gross margins well below classic software levels. That's not necessarily bad, but it changes the valuation logic. A buyer paying a software multiple for a business with services-like margins is overpaying.

**NADIA:** But the cost of AI has been falling.

**OWEN:** The price per unit of AI work, at a given capability level, has fallen dramatically over the last few years, which is good for these businesses. But two things complicate it. Customers use AI products more as they get better, and newer products use more AI per task, for example agents that take many steps to complete one job. So the total bill can go up even while the unit price goes down. In diligence, you want to see the trend in AI cost per unit of customer value, like per invoice processed or per ticket resolved, over the last several quarters.

**NADIA:** Where else does AI show up?

**OWEN:** In headcount and how it's classified. Human reviewers who check AI output might sit in operations, support or even research. If they're doing work that's essential to delivering the product, their cost belongs in cost of revenue for an honest view of gross margin. In capitalized development costs, if the company capitalizes AI development work. And in the revenue line, if the company has started selling AI features separately or with new pricing models, where you want to understand how that revenue is recognized.

**NADIA:** And for a non-software target?

**OWEN:** For a services or industrial business that uses AI internally, look at the vendor costs, the savings the company claims, and whether those savings show up in the actual labor costs. If management says AI saved twenty full-time equivalents, ask to see the headcount trend, the overtime trend and the volume trend. Claimed savings that don't show up in the numbers are a common gap.

---

### Quality of earnings in an AI world

**NADIA:** You're describing things that a quality of earnings review would normally catch.

**OWEN:** Some of them, and the quality of earnings provider should be briefed to look for them. Three AI-specific adjustments come up. First, the human cost of delivering AI, which we just covered. Second, non-recurring AI savings that management has added back to earnings in its adjusted figures, saying "we'll save this much from AI next year, so add it to this year's EBITDA." Buyers should be skeptical of pro forma AI savings that haven't happened yet.

**NADIA:** That's a classic adjusted EBITDA issue with a new label.

**OWEN:** Exactly. And third, AI-related revenue that might not be durable. For example, revenue from customers who bought a new AI product on a pilot or a short contract, or revenue from a one-off project to implement AI. That revenue might be real, but it shouldn't be valued like recurring subscription revenue.

**NADIA:** What about AI costs that might rise?

**OWEN:** That's a forward-looking point, but important. If the target uses a model at a promotional price, or under an early-customer agreement, the cost could rise at renewal. And if a model it depends on is retired, it might need to move to a more expensive one. Ask to see the AI vendor contracts and their pricing terms, which we'll come back to.

---

### Teams and talent

**NADIA:** Let's talk about people. How do you assess the AI team?

**OWEN:** Start with what the team actually does. A company might say it has an AI team of thirty, but that could mean thirty researchers training models, thirty engineers building products on top of models, or ten engineers and twenty data labelers. All of those can be legitimate, but they mean very different things for the business.

**NADIA:** What's the right profile?

**OWEN:** For most companies building AI products today, the most valuable people are engineers who understand both the domain and how to build reliable systems with AI models. People who know how to evaluate, how to handle errors, and how to integrate AI into a product customers depend on. A small team of those can be worth more than a large research group.

**NADIA:** And key person risk?

**OWEN:** It's often high in AI teams. The core AI capability may sit with two or three people, who may be in high demand in the job market. Find out who they are, what their incentives are, whether they're staying through the transaction, and whether their knowledge is documented. Retention packages for key AI staff are common in deals now.

**NADIA:** And the rest of the organization?

**OWEN:** That's the other half. How widely do the target's employees use AI in their own work? A software company whose engineers use AI coding tools heavily will develop faster than one that doesn't. A services company whose staff use AI well will be more productive. Ask about adoption of AI tools across the organization, the policy, and the results. It's a good indicator of the culture's readiness for the value creation plan.

---

### When the target isn't an AI company

**NADIA:** Most of what we've said is about targets that sell AI. But most private equity deals are for businesses that just use it. What changes?

**OWEN:** The claim question shrinks and the risk question changes shape. A distribution business, a dental group or a logistics company probably isn't claiming proprietary AI. But it's almost certainly using AI somewhere, often in ways management doesn't fully know about. So the diligence question becomes: what AI is in use, who approved it, what data does it touch, and what could go wrong?

**NADIA:** How do you find out, if management doesn't know?

**OWEN:** A few practical ways. Ask for the list of software subscriptions and look for AI tools and AI features in existing tools. Most major business software now includes AI features, often switched on by default. Ask IT for the data on which web services employees use. Ask a few team leads, in finance, sales, customer service and operations, how their teams use AI day to day. The answers are usually more interesting than the official policy.

**NADIA:** And what are you looking for?

**OWEN:** Three things. Sensitive data going into tools without proper agreements, like customer records or employee data in a consumer chatbot. Decisions being made with AI that fall under specific rules, like screening job applicants, setting individual prices or making credit decisions. And customer-facing AI that speaks for the company, like a website chatbot or an AI phone agent, where a wrong answer creates liability. None of those are usually deal-breakers. They're things to fix in the first hundred days, and to price into the plan.

**NADIA:** And the policy?

**OWEN:** Ask whether there is one, when it was written, and whether anyone follows it. An AI policy that exists only as a document nobody's read is common. What matters is whether there's an inventory, an approval process for new tools, and someone accountable. For a mid-sized company, the honest answer is often "not yet," and that's fine, as long as the buyer knows and plans for it.

**NADIA:** So for those targets, AI diligence is mostly about the upside and the hygiene.

**OWEN:** Mostly. The upside is the big question, and the hygiene is the risk. Plus the threat question, which can matter even for non-software businesses, like an outsourced call center or a translation company, where AI changes what customers are willing to pay for.

---

### Access, clean rooms and confidentiality

**NADIA:** Let's talk about the practical problem of access. Sellers don't love handing over production data and source code.

**OWEN:** They don't, and they have good reasons. In a competitive process, some bidders are competitors or own competitors. Customer data may be confidential or regulated. Source code is the crown jewels. So you have to design the access.

**NADIA:** What are the options?

**OWEN:** The first is a clean team. A small group, often the buyer's outside advisors, who can see sensitive information and report conclusions to the deal team without passing on the raw details. That's standard for competitively sensitive commercial data, and it works for AI metrics too. The second is a technical clean room, where an independent advisor gets access to the production metrics or code in a controlled environment, runs agreed analyses, and reports results.

**NADIA:** And code review?

**OWEN:** Code review is usually done by a specialist firm, sometimes with automated scanning tools for open-source licenses and security issues, and sometimes with a session where engineers walk the reviewer through the system. For AI, I'd add a walkthrough of the evaluation setup and a look at the prompts and configuration that drive the AI features, because that's where a lot of the actual product logic lives now.

**NADIA:** Prompts are product logic?

**OWEN:** In many AI products, a large share of the behavior is defined by instructions to the model, configuration and the data the system retrieves, rather than by traditional code. A technical reviewer who only reads the traditional code can miss how the product actually works. So ask to see those too, under the same confidentiality as the code.

**NADIA:** And timing?

**OWEN:** Ask early. Access negotiations take time, and the analysis takes time. If you ask for production metrics in the last week before final bids, you won't get them, and you'll end up pricing a claim you couldn't test.

---

### Reading the seller's materials

**NADIA:** Let's say you're reading the information memorandum. What phrases make you lean in?

**OWEN:** Some phrases are almost always worth a follow-up question. "Proprietary AI" is the first. Proprietary what? A model they trained? Data they own? Or a configuration of someone else's model? "AI-native" is another. It can mean the company was built around AI from day one, or it can mean they added a chatbot last year. "Fully automated," "no human in the loop," and "self-learning" are all claims that should come with evidence.

**NADIA:** And numbers?

**OWEN:** Any percentage that describes automation, accuracy or productivity gains should have a clear definition and a source. "Customers save forty percent of their time" should lead to "which customers, measured how, by whom?" And "AI revenue" or "AI-influenced revenue" should come with a definition, because some companies count any product with an AI feature as AI revenue.

**NADIA:** What about projections?

**OWEN:** Look at how much of the projected growth depends on AI products that aren't yet launched or are early. And look at the assumed pricing of those products. A plan that assumes customers will pay a large premium for AI features should be tested against what customers actually say in the reference calls.

---

### A diligence workplan

**NADIA:** Let's put it together. What does an AI diligence workplan look like for a typical deal?

**OWEN:** For a mid-sized software or tech-enabled services target, I'd structure it in three phases. In phase one, before the first round of bids, a desk review. Read the materials, assess the four questions at a high level, do a few expert calls on the market, and write a two-page view: where AI sits in the value story, the main risks, and the key questions.

**NADIA:** Phase two.

**OWEN:** After you're invited into the next round, with data room access, the deep work. The claim test with real data. The technical review of the stack, which is next episode. The threat assessment, which is episode three. Customer calls. Management interviews. The legal review of data rights, licenses and AI-related contracts. And input to the quality of earnings provider on the AI-specific adjustments.

**NADIA:** And phase three?

**OWEN:** Confirmatory, before signing. Close out open questions, review the final contract language on AI, which is episode four, and hand over the findings to the team that will build the value creation plan. That handover is often neglected, and it's a waste, because the diligence team has just learned more about the company's AI than anyone at the fund.

**NADIA:** Who does the work?

**OWEN:** Usually a mix. The deal team leads and owns the conclusions. A technical advisor, who might be a specialist firm, does the hands-on review. The commercial advisor covers the threat and the market. Legal counsel covers rights, licenses, regulation and the contract. And the fund's own operating partners or AI experts, if it has them, should be involved, especially on the upside question.

**NADIA:** And timing?

**OWEN:** Compressed, as always. A focused technical AI review can be done in two to three weeks with good data access. The danger is that AI gets a page in the general technology report, written by someone who spent a day on it. For deals where AI is central to value, that's not enough.

---

### The upside question, briefly

**NADIA:** We've spent most of today on the claim. Say a word about the fourth question, the upside, since it often drives the price.

**OWEN:** The upside question is: what could we do with AI after we own this business, and how confident are we? Diligence should produce a short list of the biggest opportunities, each with a rough size built from the target's own data, a view on difficulty, and the evidence behind it. For a software target, that might be AI features customers would pay for, cost optimization of existing AI, or engineering productivity. For a services target, it's the workflows where money leaks or skilled time is wasted.

**NADIA:** And how much rigor?

**OWEN:** Enough that the investment committee can tell the difference between an opportunity backed by the company's data and one backed by a consultant's benchmark. "Our analysis of the target's phone logs suggests eight hundred thousand to one point two million dollars of missed revenue a year" is evidence. "AI can typically deliver fifteen percent productivity gains" is not. And the upside list becomes the first draft of the value creation plan, which is another reason the diligence team and the operating team should work together from the start.

---

### Red flags and green flags

**NADIA:** Give me a list. Red flags first.

**OWEN:** Claims without data: big automation or accuracy numbers that the company can't support with production metrics. Undisclosed human work behind automated claims. No evaluations, or evaluations on test data that the model has seen. Gross margins that don't reconcile with the claimed automation. Heavy dependence on one model provider without any plan to switch. Data used for AI without clear rights. Key AI knowledge in one or two people with no retention plan. And a management team that gets defensive about any of the above.

**NADIA:** And green flags?

**OWEN:** Production metrics that are tracked and shared, broken down by customer and over time. A clear, honest description of where humans are involved and why. A real evaluation practice, with results tracked through model changes. A product whose value would survive a change of model provider. Data rights that are documented. AI costs that are understood and trending well per unit of value. And customers who can tell you, in their own words and numbers, what the AI changed for them.

**NADIA:** And the most important green flag?

**OWEN:** A team that knows the weaknesses of its own product. If the CTO can tell you, unprompted, where the AI struggles, what they're doing about it, and what it costs, that's a team you can work with. The companies to worry about are the ones that say it's all solved.

---

### Ledgerline: what the team found

**NADIA:** Let's finish the Ledgerline story. Our made-up accounts payable software company with "ninety five percent straight-through processing." What did the diligence team find?

**OWEN:** Let's say this is how it played out. The production data, run by an independent advisor in a clean room, showed that ninety five percent was the rate for invoice header fields, like vendor name, date and total, on customers who'd been live for more than six months. For full invoice coding, including the line-level general ledger codes, the rate was seventy eight percent. For new customers in their first three months, it was around sixty percent.

**NADIA:** So the headline was true, narrowly.

**OWEN:** True for a narrow definition, which is common. And the operations data showed something else. Ledgerline had a team of forty people in an offshore center who reviewed low-confidence invoices for customers on the premium plan. That wasn't hidden exactly, it was in the operations headcount, but it wasn't in the sales pitch. Their cost sat in general and administrative expenses, not in cost of revenue.

**NADIA:** Which flatters gross margin.

**OWEN:** By several points. Moving that team into cost of revenue took gross margin from seventy four percent to sixty eight. Still a good business, but a different one than the information memorandum described.

**NADIA:** And the customers?

**OWEN:** The independent customer calls were positive about the product and the support. Several customers said the line-level coding was where they still spent time. Two mentioned that their ERP vendor had announced invoice AI features, and they were watching. And none of them said they'd pay a premium for more AI. They wanted the same price for better results.

**NADIA:** So what did it mean for the deal?

**OWEN:** It didn't kill it. It changed the model and the plan. The buyer adjusted gross margin, reduced the assumed price uplift from new AI features, and added a value creation workstream to improve line-level automation, which, if it worked, would let the company shrink the review team over time. That workstream became part of the equity story the buyer would tell at exit. We'll come back to how findings like these turn into price and terms in episode four.

---

### What's next

**NADIA:** So where do we go from here?

**OWEN:** Next episode, we go under the hood. Data rights and data quality, the models and who supplies them, the cost of running them, the technical debt that AI creates, security risks specific to AI, and what a technical reviewer should actually look at in the code and the systems.

**NADIA:** Give me the takeaways from today.

**OWEN:** Four questions on every deal: threat, claim, risk and upside, scoped to how central AI is to the value. Decompose every AI claim into definitions and data, and ask for the production metrics. Look for the undisclosed human, the borrowed capability and the inflated demo. Test the product yourself where you can, and call customers the seller didn't choose. Follow AI into the financials, especially gross margin, adjusted EBITDA and headcount. And hand everything you learn to the people who'll build the plan after closing.

**NADIA:** Thanks for joining us in The AI Diligence Room. I'm Nadia.

**OWEN:** And I'm Owen. See you next time.
